summary: A content search in the window stops as soon as it is no longer wanted. Each search carries a flag that is set when another search takes its place (typing on, a switch of scope, of Name and Contents, or of the filter, Refresh, and every re-run after index, settings or file changes), when the search ends (the field cleared, Escape, going elsewhere), and when its tab or window closes. fff-search looks at the flag every few files and stops reading, and the engine leaves out the search locations it had not reached yet (new Engine::grep_cancellable; Engine::grep, `fff search` and the server are unchanged). Superseded searches no longer take fff-search's threads from the search on screen or hold the index's read lock to their end. The index status behind the sidebar footer, the status bar's indexing text and the counts in Settings is read on a background thread instead of the window's thread, where it could freeze the window behind a content search. A search no longer counts every indexed folder to learn whether an index is still being built.
changelog: A content search went on after you typed on, changed where it looked, cleared the search field, or closed its tab, until it had filled its results or reached the time limit. Several ran at once and slowed down the one you were waiting for, and with the time limit set to None they could read every file. A content search now stops as soon as the search changes or ends. Reading the file counts for the sidebar also no longer runs on the window's thread, where it could freeze the window while a content search or a scan was under way.
behaviour_changes: A content search in the window stops within a few files once another search takes its place. Before, it ran until its page of results was full or the time limit passed (5 seconds by default), or over every file with the limit set to None. What replaces it: typing on, a change of scope, a switch between Name and Contents, a filter turned on or off, Refresh, and every re-run (the retry while an index is being built, the refresh at the end of a scan, a changed search setting, result limit, hidden files or the Applications switch, files changed in the window's other tabs or pane).
It also stops when the search ends (the field cleared, Escape, going to another place) and when its tab or window closes.

The search on screen is no longer slowed by the ones before it, and changes to the index (opening a result, a batch from the file watcher) wait only for the current search. Measured in review in a debug build, where fff-search is optimised: 20,000 files of 3.7 KB, a word that is in none of them, seven searches started 8 ms apart. Before, every search read all 20,000 files and the last one answered 76 and 207 ms after it started in two runs, against 60 to 66 ms alone. After, the six superseded searches stopped after 936 to 5,096 files and the last one answered in 49 and 77 ms.

The index status is read on a background thread. It feeds the sidebar footer, the status bar's "Indexing N files…" when the sidebar is hidden, the file count of each search location in Settings, and the file count in the "Indexing…" message. A new window or tab has no status until its first reading arrives, and its footer reads "0 files indexed" until then: normally less than a frame, but as long as the reading has to wait when a change to the index is queued behind a running content search. Before, the whole window froze for that time.
After Rescan, a change of search locations, or a search-engine setting, the old counts stay until the new reading arrives. The window then redraws at once instead of at the next 400 ms tick.

Rescan: the status is asked for beside the rescan, so the first reading can already see it running. For a rescan shorter than 400 ms the refresh at its end (search run again, folder sizes, Recents, terminals) may now happen where it never did.
Name and content searches no longer count every indexed folder on each query to learn whether an index is still being built. Nothing visible.
Manual: one sentence in the "Content search time limit" row of the Search engine settings: whatever the limit, a content search that is still running stops as soon as you change the search or end it.
API: Engine::grep_cancellable(&GrepRequest, Option<&Arc<AtomicBool>>) is new. Engine::grep, `fff search` and the server are unchanged, so a content search from Nushell runs to its end as before.
left_out: The optional 250 ms pause before a contents search: the verifier dropped it, so src/finder/dialogs.rs and the manual's "50 ms" are untouched.
Name searches are not stopped. They take milliseconds and the brief is about content searches. run_search makes the flag for every search, so it is there to use.

A stopped search still makes its rows, one look at each file it found and at most as many as the result limit, before they are dropped. I added an early exit for that in review and took it out again: the saving is small, and its test had to read SearchStats::total_matched, which search-truncation-honesty removes.
No test fails without the `&& !aborted` gate on `stopped`: reaching the time limit takes at least a second of real time. `!cut.stopped` in the engine test is only a guard.
The two r.scanning() swaps have no test of their own. The meaning is the same as r.status().scanning, also when a picker is missing.
The scanning-to-idle branch of the status poll has no test: the harness cannot stage a scan. Its body is unchanged.

No before and after pictures: nothing visible changes by design, and shot.sh settles after every step, so it cannot show overlapping searches. The pictures show a contents search and Settings with the counts in place.
cargo clippy --features term was not run: src/term is untouched and calls nothing that changed (grepped, with src/macos.rs, src/win.rs and examples/).
Not compiled for macOS or Windows. No platform-specific code is touched: src/finder/mod.rs has no cfg outside its tests, and the new imports are used on every platform.
CHANGELOG.md is not edited, per the guide. The entry is in this record and in the commit message.
tests: Test hook added: Finder::search_abort_for_test, the flag of the search last started.
review_fixes: Added tests/controls.rs closing_a_tab_stops_its_contents_search. The commit message and the Changelog paragraph say a closed tab's search is stopped, and nothing tested it. It rests on the tab's browser being dropped when the tab closes, which one kept handle anywhere would undo with no other test noticing. The test opens a second tab, starts a contents search in it, keeps only the search's flag, closes the tab with Cmd+W before the search has answered, and expects the flag to be set. It fails when a dropped handle no longer sets its flag.

Reworded the doc comment on AbortOnDrop, which read "when the next search's takes its place". It now names the three moments the handle is dropped: the next search starts, the search ends, the tab closes.

Rebased onto search-skeleton-flash (bc834b7), which landed during the review. One conflict, in src/finder/mod.rs, where both changes added a test hook after rows_for_test; both are kept. Both changes' tests are in tests/controls.rs.
Nothing else was changed. The engine, the search and status code, the manual sentence and the commit message are the implementer's.
notes:
Checked. Each new test was seen to fail with its part of the change taken out. Reverse-applying the whole src and crates diff leaves tests that don't compile (they use grep_cancellable, AbortOnDrop and the test hook), so I took the behaviour out piece by piece and kept the names. The engine no longer hands the flag to fff-search: the engine test fails with "200 hits". The engine goes on to the next location after an abort: the engine test fails at "the second location isn't searched at all". content_search hands the engine no flag: its unit test fails with "200 rows". run_search doesn't replace the flag: the typing test fails at its first assertion. set_query's empty branch doesn't replace it: the typing test fails at its last. A dropped handle doesn't set its flag: the AbortOnDrop unit test, the typing test and the tab test fail. poll_index_status reads the status when it is called: the status test fails with left 0, right 4. check.sh printed CHECK OK on the trunk commit: 458 passed in 16 test binaries, 3 of 3 known root-only failures. tests/basics.rs, controls.rs, finder.rs and folder_tree.rs also pass with SEED=1, 7 and 42, apart from the known root-only test. The timing in behaviour_changes comes from a scratch test in engine.rs that is not committed; its files are deleted.

The three ways I thought this most likely to hurt a user, and what the code says.
(1) A search that is still wanted is told to stop, and its cut-short answer is shown as if it were complete. A flag belongs to one search (run_search makes a new one each time) and is set only by replacing or dropping Finder::search_abort: in run_search beside the search_gen bump, in set_query's empty branch beside the same bump, and when the browser is dropped. Nothing else writes search_abort, search_gen or search_task (grepped), and an answer whose generation has moved on returns before it touches results. So a stopped search's answer is never shown, and every stop is followed by the next search's answer or by the end of the search. That is what search-skeleton-flash asked of this change, since its placeholders and "Searching…" read `searching`.
(2) The refresh at the end of a scan is lost or doubled now that the status comes from a background read, or the footer sticks. The loop is unchanged: was_scanning from the last reading, the new one assigned, the refresh on the edge. The first reading only assigns, as the synchronous read did, so calling poll_index_status again cannot fire a second refresh. What is new is that the first reading is taken a hop after the call instead of inside it. A scan that ended between a new window's first reads of the index and that reading would go unseen by that window: folder sizes or terminals from an index that was still being built, and no refresh after. In Finder::new the status read is queued before the terminals read, and folder sizes are asked for only after the listing has come back, so the order would have to flip within microseconds. A search has its own retry while its answer says indexing, and Recents waits for the scan itself. I left it as it is.
(3) Threads pile up or a lock is held longer. A stopped search stops reading at once, but its call can return late: in my runs 1 of 12 superseded searches returned only when the newest one did, and the implementer saw 2 of 18. A fff-search pool thread that is waiting inside the stopped search takes the newest search's job and runs it on top, and the stopped one cannot return until that ends. Until then it keeps the read lock of the location it was in, which the newest search holds too unless it has moved on to another location, and one background thread. Before this change all of them ran to their end. A status read that has to wait holds one background thread per window and the engine's list of indexes for reading, as the window's thread did before with the window frozen. No lock is taken in a new order.

Doubts that remain.
1. Only Linux was built and run.
2. the_index_status_is_read_in_the_background pins that the status is not read inside the call. It empties the engine's search locations behind the window, sends Rescan without settling, and expects the old count until the hop. It is the only deterministic stand-in I found for "not on the window's thread". If a later change fills the status at once from something that takes no lock, reword it.
3. How long a new window shows "0 files indexed" can't be timed here. The reading is asked for before the first frame is presented and is normally back within it. A new tab opened while a change to the index waits behind a long content search shows it for as long as that search runs; starting a new tab with the status of the tab it was opened from would hide that.
4. How fast a search stops is fff-search's doing. It looks at the flag at every eighth file, finishes the file it is reading (up to the size limit, 10 MB by default), and can read on to the end of the chunk it is in, which grows to 8,192 files on four to eight cores. The time limit works through the same check.

For briefs still to come:
- search-truncation-honesty (next in line): the engine's loop now lives in Engine::grep_cancellable(req, abort), and grep() only calls it with None. Keep four things when you rewrite the loop: `abort_signal: abort.cloned()` in the options; `aborted` read after each root's search; `|| aborted` on the break at the end of the loop, with your deadline check beside it; and no `stopped` for a root that was aborted. Your page_end rule calls a result with next_file_offset > 0, fewer matches than the page and time left "Full (an abort from picker teardown)". With this change that case is common: the window sets the flag whenever a search is superseded. Such an answer is always thrown away by the window, so `more` on it does no harm, but it must not read as `stopped` (the engine test asserts !cut.stopped) and the roots after it must stay unsearched. content_search has a fifth parameter, `abort: &Arc<AtomicBool>`; keep handing Some(abort) to grep_cancellable. Its unit test asserts rows.len() < 50 with 200 matching files and a limit of 500, which holds with `limit + 1` and `per_file: 1`.
- regex-content-search: content_search(engine, query, scope, limit, abort); add your mode beside these and keep grep_cancellable. In Regex mode call picker.grep(&query, &options) with the loop's own options, which carry the flag. set_search_regex only has to call run_search, which replaces the flag. The server goes on calling Engine::grep.
- scoped-search-special-folder-names: the code you change is in grep_cancellable. Your second pass inside the scope, the retry when the first found nothing, must not run for a search that was told to stop: fff-search skips its own fallback then (grep.rs:223). Check the flag before the retry and use the same options for it.
- search-settings-without-effect: Engine::grep's loop is in grep_cancellable, so allow_file_size goes before root.picker.read() there. search_settings_change_content_search has a new neighbour above it.
- content-match-highlight, preview-jump-to-match: content_search has a fifth parameter (abort). A stopped search returns part of the rows and the window drops them; nothing to handle.
- adhoc-index-feedback: (a) Engine::status() no longer runs on the window's thread, but it still holds the engine's `indexes` lock for reading while it waits for a picker's lock, so cancelling only after the write guard is dropped still matters. (b) A window's content search hands fff-search its own flag, and fff-search then no longer looks at the picker's own cancel flag (file_picker.rs:1397-1400). picker.cancel() on a discarded index will not stop a window's content search that is running on it; it goes on until it is superseded, ends, or reaches the time limit. `fff search` has no flag and does stop. (c) index_status is filled a hop after poll_index_status is called. (d) In run_search's retry leave search_abort alone; only run_search and set_query's empty branch replace it.
- empty-state-messages: indexing_progress() reads index_status, which a new window has only after its first background reading and which is as old as the last 400 ms poll. search_stats.indexing is the answer's own word and is there at once.
- live-search-results: when run_search becomes start_search, keep `self.search_abort = AbortOnDrop::default()` beside the search_gen bump, for quiet runs too. Your counter bump in rescan() would make the refresh after a short Rescan certain; today it depends on whether the status poll, started beside the rescan, sees it running.
- results-scroll-reset, search-start-no-flash, back-forward-restore-search, smart-folder-save-and-leaks, query-scope-from-cli: set_query's empty branch and run_search each replace search_abort next to their search_gen bump. Keep both lines when you edit around them; typing_on_stops_the_contents_search_for_what_was_typed_before fails if either goes.
- escape-ends-search: that test presses Escape in the search field with words in it and expects the search to be over and its flag set. Both of your variants end the search through set_query(""), which is what sets it.
- sorted-search-results: your brief says a background search cannot be cancelled once started. That still holds for name searches: only content_search reads the flag. The flag is made for every search in run_search if you want it there.
- search-roots-notes-dedupe: poll_index_status no longer fills index_status when it is called; the reading arrives a hop later with its own cx.notify(). Store missing_roots in your own update as planned, and don't read the status in that update.
- tab-drop-and-close, restore-session-tabs: closing_a_tab_stops_its_contents_search expects a closed tab's browser to be dropped. If a closed tab is ever kept, to reopen it for example, end its search first, or the test fails and the search runs on. Each new or restored tab asks for the index status once, in the background.
- strict-check-scope-relative: one line of Engine::search changed: `indexing` asks r.scanning().
- files-changed-off-thread: search_gen still moves on every run_search and when the search ends, so comparing it is safe.
- stale-previews-and-cancel: AbortOnDrop in src/finder/mod.rs sets a flag when its owner replaces or drops it, if your cancellation follow-up wants one.

Found, not fixed (on the trunk before this change, except the last):
- poll_index_status, called again while a scan is being polled, takes its first reading without the refresh, as the synchronous read did. A scan that ends between the previous poll's last reading and that one (up to 400 ms) gets no refresh: folder sizes and terminals stay as they were, and a search that answered before the scan began isn't run again. It takes a search setting or the search locations changing, or Rescan, just as a scan ends.
- Engine::status() holds the engine's `indexes` lock for reading while it waits for a picker's lock. While it waits behind a content search, set_roots waits for it, and a new search can wait behind set_roots.
- The content search time limit is given to each search location in turn (time_budget_ms per root in the engine's loop). With three locations and nothing found, a search runs up to 15 seconds at the default. search-truncation-honesty's single deadline covers it.
- Rescan starts the status poll beside the rescan instead of after it. Whether a rescan shorter than 400 ms is followed by the refresh depends on which of the two runs first. Before this change it never was.
- From this change: a stopped content search can return late, as (3) says. fff-search runs each search with rayon's install, and a pool thread waiting in one search can take another search's whole job on top of it.
